q: Does the DDRi effect really diminish with both dose and LET as independent physical observations, or is the twin attenuation a topological consequence of the single UNIVERSE ansatz that RSF multiplies only K_iDSB while K_cDSB is invariant?
basis: In UNIVERSE both attenuations (dose and LET) fall out of one algebraic choice: RSF acts only on K_iDSB, and clustered lesions dominate at high dose and high LET. They are not independent measurements. The paper's headline mechanistic prediction is therefore identifiable with the model's single invariance assumption; a genuinely independent test of the two attenuations against experimental data is not on record. If K_cDSB is actually also modulated by DDRi (e.g. because clustered lesions shift toward MMEJ, which is Pol-theta/ligase-III-dependent and thus outside the ATM/DNA-PK axis targeted by ATMi/DNA-PKi), the observed twin attenuation could be qualitatively preserved by the correct biology but with different absolute values than UNIVERSE predicts.
next_steps: 1. Request from the Heidelberg group the raw helium SOBP surviving-fraction tables (cell line x depth x dose x SF +- SD) that underlie Fig. 3-5 of the target paper. 2. For each cell-line/depth stratum, jointly fit two RSFs -- one on K_iDSB and one on K_cDSB -- and test whether the K_cDSB-RSF is statistically zero (likelihood-ratio vs. UNIVERSE's one-RSF model). 3. Run isogenic ATMi vs. DMSO pairs across an LET ladder (2, 30, 60, 120 keV/um) at fixed dose (4 Gy), fit the two-RSF variant, and use AIC/BIC to distinguish. 4. If K_cDSB-RSF differs significantly from zero at any LET, redo the RBE-ratio-vs-LET prediction with both parameters free and compare to the paper's Fig. 5.

q: Is the peak of RBE_DDRi / RBE_no-DDRi at LET ~= 30 keV/um a physical prediction, or a topological consequence of the assumed giant-loop count (~3000 loops of 2 Mbp) inherited from the Yokota/Sachs geometry?
basis: The GLOBLE geometry hard-codes ~3000 loops of ~2 Mbp. The LET at which the RBE-ratio peaks is exactly the LET where typical DSB counts per loop cross from 1 (iDSB regime) to >=2 (cDSB regime). That crossover depends only on the loop count and loop size, both of which are inputs, not derived quantities. If real chromatin topology is cell-line specific (e.g. via Hi-C-derived TAD sizes for H460 and H1437), the peak LET may shift by tens of keV/um -- which would blunt the paper's clinical guidance about which LET regimes benefit from DDRi.
next_steps: 1. In universe_smoke.py, add a grid over loop count in {1000, 3000, 6000, 12000} and loop size in {0.5, 1, 2, 4} Mbp; report peak LET and peak height as a 4x4 heatmap. 2. Pull Hi-C-derived contact-domain distributions for H460 and H1437 (both have published Hi-C from Encode/Roadmap or GEO); replace the flat 2-Mbp loop geometry with the empirical TAD-size distribution. 3. Compare the empirical-topology-driven peak LET against the geometric-default peak LET. 4. Design an experiment (e.g. RBE-ratio measurement at LET = 15, 30, 60 keV/um in three cell lines with distinct Hi-C domain-size distributions) that could falsify the geometry-independent prediction.

q: What is the correct pharmacological form of RSF vs. inhibitor concentration -- linear, Michaelis-Menten, or Hill -- and does it saturate at a physiologically achievable concentration?
basis: Liew 2019 Table 3 tabulates RSF only at 3 or 4 discrete inhibitor concentrations per line (e.g. ATMi at 0, 100, 200, 500 nM). UNIVERSE treats RSF as a per-condition input -- it does not model the dose-response of the inhibitor itself. In the clinic, physicians choose drug plasma concentration, not RSF. Without a plasma-concentration -> RSF map, the paper's clinical-translation claim (C8) is unactionable and cannot be checked against phase-I PK/PD data. In addition, if RSF saturates below the tumour-achievable plasma concentration, the mechanistic ceiling of DDRi + particle is much lower than a linear extrapolation from the 4-point ladder would suggest.
next_steps: 1. Fit Hill, Michaelis-Menten, and linear forms to the H460 and H1437 ATMi RSF ladders; report AIC and 95% CIs on the saturation parameter. 2. Overlay the fitted RSF(plasma_conc) with published PK/PD data for AZD1390 and AZD0156 (both have phase-I plasma-concentration profiles at approved schedules). 3. Add a plasma_conc -> RSF plug-in to universe_smoke.py that lets a user specify a drug schedule and returns a time-averaged SF. 4. Re-run the C8 clinical vignette (using an open TPS surrogate; see Q5) at three realistic drug schedules and report whether the DDRi + particle vs. DDRi + photon ordering is schedule-invariant.

q: Is the invariance of K_cDSB under DDR interference consistent with the biology of NHEJ vs. MMEJ repair of clustered lesions, or is it a modelling convenience that breaks down at high LET where clustered damage dominates?
basis: UNIVERSE's central mechanistic assumption for the ion-beam prediction is that DDRi does not modulate K_cDSB. Biologically, this is a strong claim: clustered DSBs are known to shift toward MMEJ (Pol-theta + LIG3) when canonical NHEJ (DNA-PKcs) is inhibited. If DDRi shifts the balance in the MMEJ direction, K_cDSB will change with DDRi, and the peak-then-fall shape of the RBE-ratio may be quantitatively wrong precisely in the LET regime where the paper claims clinical relevance. Scholz 2020 LEM-IV explicitly models cluster complexity but does not have an MMEJ-competition term either; a genuine test would distinguish the two.
next_steps: 1. Perform the H460 ATMi experiment with a Pol-theta inhibitor (novobiocin at Pol-theta-selective doses, or ART558) at LET = 100 keV/um; UNIVERSE predicts SF-ratio DDRi/no-DDRi identical to the DNA-PKcs axis alone, while MMEJ competition predicts divergent SF-ratios. 2. Extend universe_smoke.py with a cluster-complexity-dependent K_cDSB (function of local DSB density per loop) and a repair-pathway-availability multiplier; refit the LET sweep and compare AIC. 3. Reconcile the extended-UNIVERSE prediction with LEM-IV predictions at the same LET, on the same 5 cell lines. 4. Use isogenic Pol-theta-KO cell lines (published in Ceccaldi 2015) to hard-test the MMEJ-competition hypothesis at LET = 30 and 100 keV/um.

q: Does the paper's clinical claim (C8) -- that DDRi + particle preserves the therapeutic window better than DDRi + photon -- survive when patient-scale heterogeneity is added: LET_d spectra, organ-at-risk proximity, hypoxic sub-volumes, and inter-fraction repair?
basis: UNIVERSE as published treats a single homogeneous target voxel. Real patient plans have LET_d spectra (mixed low + high LET across the voxel), organ-at-risk voxels immediately adjacent to the CTV, hypoxic sub-volumes (the paper's own Liew 2020 extension), and multi-fraction repair kinetics between fractions (Liew 2022). C8's recalculation, as summarised in the abstract, does not obviously integrate any of these. The clinical implication may not survive realistic patient-scale integration, and the therapeutic-window ordering could flip in OAR-limited or hypoxia-heavy cases.
next_steps: 1. Reproduce the paper's patient vignette using an open TPS surrogate (MatRad + FLUKA-compatible LET_d maps) on a public phantom (TG-119 IMRT credentialling phantom or CORT dataset), matching the paper's target volume geometry as closely as possible. 2. Add UNIVERSE-hypoxia (Liew 2020: HRF with m = 2.94, K = 0.129%) as a voxel-level modifier of alpha_DSB, using a published hypoxia probability map for a representative head-and-neck or pancreas case. 3. Add UNIVERSE-repair kinetics (Liew 2022) between fractions of a hypofractionated schedule (5 x 8 Gy vs. 30 x 2 Gy). 4. Report therapeutic-index (TCP - NTCP) for four scenarios: {photon, particle} x {no DDRi, DDRi} with and without each of the three added realism layers. 5. Flag any scenario in which the DDRi + particle > DDRi + photon ordering flips, and identify the driver.
